data.cultural_impact: The name Zamurad is derived from the Arabic word "Zamur," meaning steadfast or resolute. This would suggest that individuals bearing this name are expected to embody the qualities of strength, determination, and unwavering commitment. In many Islamic cultures, a strong character and unyielding spirit have been highly prized, which would make the name Zamurad particularly valuable. This may have led to Zamurads being seen as leaders and role models in their communities.
data.spiritual_significance: In the Islamic faith, being steadfast and resolute in one's beliefs and actions is considered a key component of religious devotion. The name Zamurad can be seen as a reminder of this duty. Additionally, the name may be seen as reflecting the divine attributes of Allah, such as His steadfastness and consistent actions in the universe. Moreover, when used as a personal name, it serves as a constant reminder to its bearer to strive towards a strong and unwavering faith and to embody the qualities associated with the name.

historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Ibn Khaldun, Al-'Ibar, Kitab al-'ibar, Volume 3, page 294 The name Zamurad carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.context: Zamurrad ibn Qutlumush was a Mongol ruler who converted to Islam and reigned over the eastern part of what is now Iran. He was a vassal of Timoor (Timur) and a grandson of Qutlumush. Zamurrad is most famous for his role in the Battle of Angora (Ankara) in 1402, where he led the Mongol forces and was defeated by the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed I.

historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Al-Maqrizi, The History of the Prophet Muhammad, page 181 The name Zamurad carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.context: Zamurad (also known as Sultan Zamurrad Shah) was a Mongol ruler who ruled in Transoxania (present-day Uzbekistan) around the late 14th century. He was a great patron of learning and the arts, and during his reign, the city of Samarkand flourished as a cultural and intellectual center. The famous astronomer Ulugh Beg, who built the impressive observatory in Samarkand, was a vassal of Zamurad.
